newsitem.title: USA: No policy tilt in Beige Book format - Fed economist.
newsitem.headline: No policy tilt in Beige Book format - Fed economist.

text.p: The reference to the performance of wages and prices -- rather than to the economy -- at the top of the Federal Reserve's Beige Book is no hint of the monetary policy decision the U.S. central bank will take later this month, a senior Fed economist said on Wednesday.

"There is no specific format for the Beige Book. I wanted to highlight first what most people were interested in," said Cleveland Fed senior economist Michael Bryan who compiled the Beige Book issued on Wednesday. Bryan responded to a question about concerns regarding the reporting sequence in the report.
"I summarized the Beige Books of the 12 Fed banks as best as I could. There is absolutely no implications for monetary policy on the sequence of reporting," Bryan stressed.

The Treasury market responded favorably to the Beige Book that reported signs of rising wages associated with steady prices in an overall healthy U.S. economy. Bonds erased early losses on the report that presented "inconclusive evidence" regarding an eventual acceleration of inflation.
The Beige Book -- or latest assessment on U.S. economic and business conditions -- is prepared by the 12 Fed banks, and compiled by one of them on a rotating basis.
The Beige Book is prepared for discussion at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting. It was the Cleveland Fed's turn to compile the report for the September 24 FOMC meeting.

"What seemed to be the central theme in the original reports is that the inflation indicators were mixed," Bryan said. "When you looked at the wage data, you got the impression of more upward pressure than when looking at the price data."

Another report prepared by Fed economists for discussion at the FOMC is the Green Book or the Fed Board staff's economic projections. While the Beige Book relies on anecdotal evidence, the Green Book uses data and models to infer its direction.

"In not one report was somebody saying that either finished good prices or industrial prices were accelerating," added Bryan who explained he did not lead his summary with a description of the economy "because the real economy was a non-event."
"The economy looked pretty strong, similar to what it has looked like in the previous reports. The order seemed to me to make perfect sense and there is nothing more to it," Bryan concluded.
